question:
A 13-month-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic by her mother due to progressive abdominal distension, poor feeding, and failure to thrive. The perinatal history was uneventful. The family emigrated from Sudan 8 years ago. The vital signs include: temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure 100/55 mm Hg, and pulse 99/min. The physical examination shows conjunctival pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, and parietal and frontal bossing of the skull. The laboratory test results are as follows:
Hemoglobin     8.7 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 62 μm3
Red cell distribution width 12.2% (normal value is 11.5–14.5%)
Reticulocyte count    2.1 %
Leucocyte count     10,200/mm3
Platelet count   392,000/mm3
The peripheral blood smear shows microcytic red cells, target cells, and many nucleated red cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Microcytic red cells, target cells, and nucleated red cells on peripheral blood smear" -> "Hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, Mean corpuscular volume 62 μm3" -> "Reticulocyte count 2. -> 1%
CHAIN: "Conjunctival pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, parietal and frontal bossing of the skull" -> "Hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, Mean corpuscular volume 62 μm3" -> "Possible chronic hemolytic anemia" -> 60%
CHAIN: "Family emigrated from Sudan 8 years ago" -> "Possible genetic predisposition to certain hemoglobinopathies prevalent in the region" -> "Consider thalassemia or sickle cell disease" -> 50%
analysis: The clinical presentation of progressive abdominal distension, poor feeding, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, and the laboratory findings of microcytic red cells, target cells, and nucleated red cells are indicative of a severe form of anemia. The low hemoglobin level, low mean corpuscular volume, and the presence of nucleated red cells suggest a hypoproliferative anemia. Given the patient's age, emigration from an endemic region, and the presence of hepatosplenomegaly, the most likely diagnosis is Beta-thalassemia major.
